title: EVANGELOS TZAMALIS AND OTHERS v. GREECE
summary:
In Evangelos Tzamalis and Others v. Greece, the applicants—Evangelos Tzamalis, Emmanouil Tzamalis, Kostas Petropoulos, and Sofia Markopoulou—are Greek nationals of Roma origin, represented by the Greek Helsinki Monitor. Their case was brought against the Greek state, highlighting the persistent vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to forced evictions and inadequate housing protections. The applicants, along with other Roma families, moved in late 2005 from Megara (Attica) to the Kladissos area in Crete, where they set up makeshift homes on unused public and private land. Local authorities deemed their living conditions unsanitary and, after complaints from landowners and officials, police and municipal workers demolished several of their sheds in July 2006, warning that further evictions would follow. The applicants, supported by an NGO, lodged criminal complaints alleging racially motivated eviction, destruction of property, and lack of alternative accommodation, but these were dismissed by Greek prosecutors on procedural grounds, including late filing and lack of proper authorisation at the time of the first complaint.

The European Court of Human Rights examined alleged violations of Articles 3, 6, 8, 13, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, but ultimately declared the application inadmissible. The Court found that the applicants had not exhausted all available domestic remedies, as required by Article 35 of the Convention, due to procedural errors in their appeals. This case underscores the procedural barriers Roma and Traveller communities often face when seeking redress for housing rights violations, reflecting a broader historical context of marginalisation and legal obstacles in Europe.
